blog:posts.title: The Art of Slow Software: Crafting Digital Tools That Age With Grace
blog:posts.excerpt: A manifesto for permanence, tactile ergonomics and intentional engineering in an era of disposable features.

data.text: In an era dominated by ephemeral feature bloat and disposable software, there is quiet rebellion in building interfaces designed to endure like fine mid-century woodwork.
The tools we love most — a good pen, a well-balanced chisel, an editor configured over a decade — reward the opposite of novelty: stillness.
The patina of use
Physical objects gain character as they age. Software rarely does. What would it mean to design for the tenth year of use rather than the first ten minutes?
Good tools disappear into the work. Great tools make the work feel inevitable.

items.content: Data formats that outlive the application

data.title: A small exercise
data.text: Open the oldest tool you still use every day. Ask what it never changed.
Building for decades
Weniger, aber besser — less, but better.
data.caption: Dieter Rams

data.text: Slowness is not the absence of progress. It is progress you can keep.

blog:posts.title: Tactile Interfaces in a Glass-Screen World
blog:posts.excerpt: Why the click of a mechanical switch still matters, and what touchscreens forgot about feedback.

data.text: Run your finger across a modern phone and it answers with nothing: no edge, no detent, no resistance. We traded texture for flexibility, and it was mostly a good trade.
Feedback is information
A switch that clicks tells you the action happened. A screen that changes colour asks you to look. That difference compounds across thousands of interactions a day.

items.content: Make state changes audible or visible within 100ms
Give destructive actions physical weight — a hold, a second step
Keep targets where the hand expects them

data.text: The best interface you ever used was probably a light switch.

blog:posts.title: Notes on Analog Rituals
blog:posts.excerpt: Morning pages, paper calendars and the surprising productivity of friction.

data.text: Every morning begins the same way: coffee, a notebook, three pages of whatever arrives. Nothing I write there is good. That is the point.
Friction as a feature
Paper is slow. You cannot search it, sync it or share it. Those limits are exactly what make it a place to think instead of a place to perform.
The pen is the tongue of the mind.
data.caption: Miguel de Cervantes

items.content: Keep a paper calendar for one week
End the day by crossing out, not adding

blog:posts.title: Typography as Architecture
blog:posts.excerpt: Optical sizes, vertical rhythm, and building a page the way you would build a room.

data.text: A page is a room you walk through with your eyes. Margins are its walls, line length its corridor, the baseline grid its floor.
Rhythm before decoration
Set the body size and line height first, then derive every other space from them. Headings, lists and images then fall into place instead of being nudged into it.

data.title: Rule of thumb
data.text: Keep body text between 60 and 75 characters per line. Wider, and the eye loses its way home.

blog:posts.title: Designing Systems That Say No
blog:posts.excerpt: Constraints are a feature. A design system earns trust by what it refuses to include.

data.text: Every component library starts generous and ends bloated. The ones that last are the ones that learned to refuse.
Saying no, kindly

items.content: Name the problem a component solves before you build it
Prefer one flexible pattern to three rigid ones

data.text: A design system is a promise about what will not change.
Constraints free a team to spend its creativity on the work, not on rediscovering the button.

blog:posts.title: The Quiet Desk
blog:posts.excerpt: A short note on keeping one surface in your life completely clear.

data.text: One surface, nothing on it but what today needs. It is the cheapest productivity system there is, and the hardest to keep.
Try it for a week. Notice what you reach for, and what you never miss.
